bib.title: Building Applications with AI Agents, Chapter 6. Knowledge and Memory

question: How should an agent be given knowledge beyond its weights and memory of its own history, from rolling windows to semantic memory, RAG and GraphRAG?
contributions: Survey of memory approaches for agents: rolling context window, BM25 full-text search, vector-store semantic memory, RAG, semantic experience memory, GraphRAG with knowledge graphs, note-taking.

results.claim: Long-context models do not make retrieval obsolete: RAG can outperform pure long-context models on fact-seeking and enterprise queries, and production systems combine long windows with selective retrieval.
results.setup: Community consensus asserted without data, mid-2025 models (Gemini 2.5, GPT-4.1).
results.quote:
even with multipage context windows, RAG can out‐
perform pure long-context models on fact-seeking queries and enterprise
use cases

limits: No experiments or measurements anywhere in the chapter; all performance statements are assertions.
Code listings are truncated or inconsistent in the PDF text (e.g. the vectordb and LangGraph example never uses the retrieved results in the graph).
Model context figures (GPT-5, Claude 3.7 Sonnet 272,000 tokens) are mid-2025 and dated.
GraphRAG algorithm details are explicitly not covered.
Conclusion mentions 'working memory' and dynamic knowledge graphs; the chapter's note-taking section is the only working-memory material.
practices: Start with a rolling (FIFO) context window; it is easy and enough for many cases, but relevant information is lost as soon as it is ejected (Managing Context Windows).
Put the most relevant context close to the end of the prompt to raise the chance it is used (Managing Context Windows).
Use BM25 over an inverted index to inject top-K historical passages instead of the whole history (Traditional Full-Text Search).
Use embeddings in a vector store when meaning, not exact words, should match (Semantic Memory and Vector Stores).
Chunk documents, embed chunks and index them for RAG; retrieve at query time and feed the result with the question to the generator (Retrieval-Augmented Generation).
Reserve part of the context window for the best semantic-experience-memory matches, then fill the rest with system message, latest input and recent interactions (Semantic Experience Memory).
Move to GraphRAG when standard chunking and vector retrieval hit limits on multi-document or thematic questions, accepting higher cost and complexity (Using Knowledge Graphs).
Build knowledge graphs in eight steps: collect, preprocess, entity extraction, relationship extraction, ontology, population, integration and validation, maintenance (Building Knowledge Graphs).
For dynamic knowledge graphs use automated validation, scalable architecture, encryption and access controls, and human oversight (Promise and Peril of Dynamic Knowledge Graphs).
Prompt the model to write notes on the context before the question, and interleave them with the context (Note-Taking).
